questions.stem: What is the molar mass of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2? [Ca = 40, O = 16, H = 1]
questions.explanation: The subscript 2 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside it, so the formula contains one Ca, two O and two H. Molar mass = 40 + 2(16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74 g/mol.

distractorRationale.b: Only the hydrogen was doubled, giving 40 + 16 + 2
distractorRationale.d: The calcium was doubled as well, giving 80 + 34

questions.stem: How many moles of carbon dioxide are present in 88 g of CO2? [C = 12, O = 16]
questions.explanation: The molar mass of CO2 is 12 + (2 x 16) = 44 g/mol. Using n = m / M gives n = 88 / 44 = 2 mol. As a check, 88 g is twice 44 g, so it must be twice one mole.

distractorRationale.a: The division was inverted, giving 44 divided by 88
distractorRationale.c: A molar mass of 22 was used, as if only one oxygen atom were present and halved
distractorRationale.d: The molar mass was quoted instead of the number of moles

questions.stem: How many molecules are contained in 0.5 mol of oxygen gas? [NA = 6.02 x 10^23 per mole]
questions.explanation: Number of particles = number of moles x Avogadro constant, so N = 0.5 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 3.01 x 10^23 molecules. Half a mole must contain half of the Avogadro constant, which is a quick way to check the answer.

distractorRationale.c: This is the number in one full mole, ignoring the 0.5 factor
distractorRationale.d: The 0.5 was used as a multiplier of 2 instead of a half
